questions.questionText: Why does fitting a scaler on the entire dataset before splitting into train/test cause data leakage?
options: It doesn't cause any problem, fitting order doesn't matter
The scaler's statistics (mean, variance) are computed using test set data too, so information about the test set leaks into what the model effectively sees
It makes the model train faster
It only affects regression models, never classification
questions.correctAnswer: The scaler's statistics (mean, variance) are computed using test set data too, so information about the test set leaks into what the model effectively sees
questions.explanation: Since the scaler is fit using test-set values, the transformed test set is no longer truly "unseen" — its own statistics helped shape the transformation, inflating reported performance versus real-world deployment.

questions.questionText: Why can accuracy alone be a misleading metric to optimize for on an imbalanced dataset?
options: Accuracy is always the correct metric regardless of class balance
A model that mostly predicts the majority class can score high accuracy while performing very poorly on the minority class, which aggregate accuracy hides
Accuracy cannot be computed on imbalanced data
Imbalanced data makes accuracy impossible to interpret at all
questions.correctAnswer: A model that mostly predicts the majority class can score high accuracy while performing very poorly on the minority class, which aggregate accuracy hides
questions.explanation: This is the same trap from the classification-metrics lesson: high aggregate accuracy can coexist with very poor minority-class recall, which per-class metrics expose and accuracy alone hides.

questions.questionText: Why does repeatedly checking test-set performance while trying different hyperparameters invalidate the final reported test score?
options: It doesn't invalidate anything, this is standard practice
The test set effectively becomes a second training set once it's used to make decisions, so it no longer measures true generalization to unseen data
Hyperparameter tuning should always use the test set directly
This only matters for deep learning models, not classical ML
questions.correctAnswer: The test set effectively becomes a second training set once it's used to make decisions, so it no longer measures true generalization to unseen data
questions.explanation: Once a test set has influenced any decision (like which hyperparameter to pick), it's no longer an unbiased measure of generalization — cross-validation within the training data is the correct way to tune hyperparameters instead.
